'''''Muscari''''' is a [[genus]] of [[perennial]] [[bulb]]ous plants native to [[Eurasia]] that produce spikes of dense, most commonly blue, urn-shaped [[flower]]s resembling bunches of [[grape]]s in the spring. The common name for the genus is '''grape hyacinth''', but they should not be confused with [[hyacinth]]s. A number of species of ''Muscari'' are used as [[Ornamental plant|ornamental]] garden plants.

==Description==
[[Brian Mathew]] says that many species of grape hyacinths are difficult to distinguish.<ref name=Mathew1987>{{Citation |last=Mathew |first=Brian |year=1987 |title=The Smaller Bulbs |location=London |publisher=B.T. Batsford |isbn=978-0-7134-4922-8 }}, pp. 124–130</ref> They usually have one or more narrow leaves which arise from a bulb. The flowers appear in the spring and form a spike or [[raceme]], being held in a close or loose spiral around a central stalk. The flowers often become less tightly spaced as the flower matures. The flower colour varies from pale blue to a very dark blue, almost black in some cases (albino forms are also known). In some species, the upper flowers may be of a colour or shape different from the lower flowers. Individual flowers are composed of six fused tepals forming a spherical to obovoid shape, constricted at the end to form a mouth around which the ends of the tepals show as small lobes or "teeth", which may be of a color different from the rest of the tepal.<ref name=Mathew1987/>

==Taxonomy==
[[File:Muscaris-J.Eudes-06.JPG|thumb|[[Botanical illustration|Illustration]] by Eugène-Jules Eudes, 1929]]The use of ''muscari'' as part of the name of at least some of the species included in the modern genus can be traced back to [[Carolus Clusius]] in 1601, long before the modern [[International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi, and plants|rules of botanical nomenclature]] were established.<ref name=GarbariGreuter1970>{{Citation |last1=Garbari |first1=F. |last2=Greuter |first2=W. |year=1970 |title=On the Taxonomy and Typification of Muscari Miller (Liliaceae) and Allied Genera, and on the Typification of Generic Names |journal=Taxon |volume=19 |issue=3 |pages=329–335 |doi=10.2307/1219056 |jstor=1219056 |bibcode=1970Taxon..19..329G |name-list-style=amp }}</ref> In 1753, [[Carl Linnaeus]] used the name ''Hyacinthus muscari'' for the plant now called ''[[Muscari racemosum]]''.<ref name=KewWC_Mr>{{Citation |author=WCSP |year=2011 |title=World Checklist of Selected Plant Families |publisher=The Board of Trustees of the [[Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew]] |url=http://apps.kew.org/wcsp/home.do |access-date=2011-11-14 }}, search for "Muscari racemosum"</ref> In 1754 [[Philip Miller]] formally established the genus ''Muscari'' according to modern rules of nomenclature.<ref name=GarbariGreuter1970/> The name ''muscari'' comes from the Greek ''{{Lang|el|muschos}}'', musk, referring to the scent.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Hyam |first1=R. |last2=Pankhurst |first2=R.J. |year=1995 |title=Plants and their names : a concise dictionary |location=Oxford |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-866189-4 |name-list-style=amp }}, p. 330</ref> Miller did not designate a type species, although the etymology of the genus name points to the species Linnaeus called ''Hyacinthus muscari'' (a.k.a. ''Muscari racemosum'').<ref name=GarbariGreuter1970/> Britton & Brown (1913), Garbari & Greuter (1970), Speta (1982), and Böhnert ''et al.'' (2023) accept ''Muscari botryoides'' as the type species.<ref name = Bohnert>Böhnert, T., Neumann, M., Quandt, D. and Weigend, M. (2023), Phylogeny based generic reclassification of ''Muscari'' sensu lato (Asparagaceae) using plastid and genomic DNA. ''Taxon'', 72: 261-277. https://doi.org/10.1002/tax.12864</ref>

Classified in the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Asparagaceae]], subfamily [[Scilloideae]],<ref>{{citation |last=Stevens |first=P.F.  |title=Angiosperm Phylogeny Website: Asparagales: Scilloideae |url=http://www.mobot.org/mobot/research/apweb/orders/asparagalesweb.htm#Hyacinthaceae }}</ref> the genus was formerly placed in the [[Liliaceae]] as a member of the tribe [[Hyacintheae]]. The genus was at one time divided into four groups or subgenera: ''Botryanthus'', ''Pseudomuscari'', ''Leopoldia'', and ''Muscarimia''.<ref name=Mathew1987/> Some authorities recognize ''Leopoldia'' and ''Pseudomuscari'' as separate genera. {{As of|2025|September}}, ''[[Plants of the World Online]]'' continued to recognize ''[[Muscarimia]]'' as a separate genus, with two species – ''Muscarimia macrocarpa'' and ''M. muscari'' (syn. ''Muscari racemosum'').<ref name=POWO_24537-1>{{cite web |title=''Muscarimia'' Kostel. ex Losinsk. |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:24537-1 |website=[[Plants of the World Online]] |publisher=[[Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew]] |access-date=9 July 2025}}</ref>

===Subgenera===
In 2023, Böhnert ''et al.'' published the results of a phylogenetic analysis of ''Muscari'' and its segregate genera. They found ''Muscari'' a "very natural group", with five distinct clades, which they recognize as subgenera:<ref name = Bohnert/>
*[[Muscari subg. Leopoldia|''M.'' subg. ''Leopoldia'']] <small>(Parl.) Peterm.</small>, syn. ''Leopoldia'' <small>Parl.</small>
*''M.'' subg. ''Muscari''
*''M.'' subg. ''Muscarimia'' <small>(Kostel. ex. Losinsk.) Böhnert</small>, syn. ''[[Muscarimia]]'' <small>Kostel. ex. Losinsk.</small>
*[[Muscari subg. Pseudomuscari|''M.'' subg. ''Pseudomuscari'']] <small>(Losinsk.) D.C.Stuart</small>, syn. ''Pseudomuscari'' <small>Losinsk.</small>
*''M.'' subg. ''Pulchella'' <small>Böhnert</small> – a new grouping

Böhnert et al. placed two species in ''Muscari'' subg. ''Muscarimia'' that {{As of|2025|September|lc=yes}} Plants of the World Online placed in the genus ''[[Muscarimia]]'':<ref name = Bohnert/><ref name=POWO_24537-1/>
*''[[Muscari macrocarpum]]'' <small>Sweet</small> = ''Muscarimia macrocarpa''
*''[[Muscari racemosum]]'' <small>(L.) Mill.</small> = ''Muscarimia muscari''

The names of some of the species are somewhat confused, especially in the horticultural literature. Thus the name ''M. racemosum'' is commonly found as an incorrect synonym for ''M. neglectum'', with ''M. muscarimi'' or ''M. moschatum'' being used for the true ''M. racemosum''.<ref>See, e.g., {{Harvnb|Mathew|1987}}</ref> ''Muscari fatmacereniae'' was recently described from Turkey.<ref>{{Cite journal |lang=en |last=Eker |first= İsmai̇l |date= 2019-03-14 |title=''Muscari fatmacereniae'' (Asparagaceae, Scilloideae), a new species from southern Anatolia|url=https://biotaxa.org/Phytotaxa/article/view/phytotaxa.397.1.10 |journal= Phytotaxa |volume= 397 |issue= 1 |pages= 99–106 |doi= 10.11646/phytotaxa.397.1.10 |bibcode=2019Phytx.397...99E |s2cid=92768403 |issn=1179-3163 |url-access= subscription }}</ref>

==Distribution==
The genus ''Muscari'' originated in the [[Old World]], and is native to the Mediterranean basin, central and Southern Europe, Northern Africa, Western, Central and Southwest Asia. It has become naturalized elsewhere, including Northern Europe and the United States.<ref name="POWO_24537-1" />

==Cultivation==
Some species are among the earliest garden flowers to bloom in the spring. They are planted as [[bulb]]s and tend to multiply quickly ([[naturalization (biology)|naturalise]]) when planted in good soils. They prefer well drained sandy soil, that is acid to neutral and not too rich. Naturally found in woodlands or meadows, they are commonly cultivated in lawns, borders, rock gardens and containers. They require little feeding or watering in the summer, and sun or light shade.{{citation needed|date=November 2011}}

The [[National Plant Collection|UK National Collection]] of Muscari is held by Richard Hobbs at his Witton Lane garden in [[Little Plumstead]], [[Norfolk]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://muscaricollection.com/muscari-collection |title=The National Collection of Muscari at Witton Lane |date=31 July 2019 |publisher=Norfolk Plant Heritage |access-date=23 October 2021}}</ref>
